item.title: The Death of Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie’s Child Changed Her View of Nigeria
item.description:
The writer Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie and her husband were spending the holidays at their home in Lagos, Nigeria, last December when one of their twin sons came down with what seemed to be a cold. The child, Nkanu, was 21 months old — “precious” and “a funny baby,” in the words of his father, Ivara Esege. He was still playful, but when he developed a fever, Esege, who is a physician, started him on antibiotics.

By New Year’s Day, Nkanu had not improved, so the couple took him to a local children’s hospital. Concerned that he might have atypical Kawasaki disease, a childhood illness that can lead to heart attacks and strokes, Esege also contacted Johns Hopkins Hospital, near the couple’s American home in suburban Maryland. Johns Hopkins agreed to take Nkanu as a patient, but doctors there asked for additional tests to make sure he was safe to travel. Adichie and Esege took Nkanu to Euracare, another hospital in Lagos, for the examination.

The child was sedated with Propofol, a common anesthetic, to keep him still during an M.R.I. of his brain. Adichie was waiting outside when a doctor hurried past her into the cath lab. It was alarming: Why was he rushing to the room where Nkanu was having his test done? She waited in “pure panic,” she said, until the doctor returned. “He was very calm and he said to me, ‘Well, look, they gave him too much Propofol,’” Adichie recalled. “Those were his exact words, which I will never forget until the day I die.”

Nkanu had gone into cardiac arrest. Within 24 hours — it is not clear exactly when — he was dead.

Adichie and Esege told me this story in July, at their home in Maryland. On the table, there was a tray of healthy snacks: bowls of fresh cherries, another bowl of seeds and dried fruit. Adichie, 48, was dressed in a plain, loosefitting dress, her hair combed into two simple braids. Esege, tall with a curly salt-and-pepper Afro, wore a yellow T-shirt and gym shorts. He is 57 and, like his wife, a native of Nigeria.

There was an easy choreography between the couple, but also a palpable weariness. Leading me to the dining room, where we spoke for several hours, they moved slowly, as if bereavement were a kind of arthritis, pain carried in the bones. The house was more than quiet. Their daughter, age 10, was at day camp, and the younger of the twin boys was upstairs, sleeping. (The couple asked The New York Times not to use their children’s names to protect their privacy.)

Adichie and Esege still struggle to understand how their child could have died so suddenly and inexplicably. They have urged a coroner’s court to conduct an inquest — and the court is doing so — in hopes that they can help other Nigerians who have been harmed by the country’s troubled health care system but lack the means and influence to push for change. They stress that they are not suing the hospital or the doctors and just want a better health care system.

“That’s the only thing we can try and do just to help,” Esege told me. “Hopefully someone else will not have to go through this.”

The pain of Nkanu’s death has complicated Adichie’s relationship with Nigeria. The country, with its mix of resilience, vibrancy, corruption and economic desperation, is a vivid milieu in her work, exerting a strong magnetic pull on characters who leave.

In her best-known novel, “Americanah,” the main character, Ifemelu, is a young Nigerian woman who, much like the author, comes to the United States to study and live, only to experience exhaustion and alienation that feels like “cement in her soul.” Nigeria, Adichie writes, was “where she was supposed to be, the only place she could sink her roots in without the constant urge to tug them out and shake off the soil.”

Now Adichie feels uprooted. “My feelings toward Nigeria have changed,” she said. Her son’s death was the first irrevocable loss, her native country the second.

Health care in Nigeria suffers from relatively low government support, limited infrastructure and an exodus of skilled workers. According to a recent estimate from the World Bank, Nigeria has 0.4 doctors for every 1,000 people (the figure is 3.7 in the United States).

But Adichie said she had confidence in Euracare, which she was told was run by international standards. “It was kind of paraded as one of the best hospitals in Lagos,” she explained.

As it happened, she knew the doctor who spoke to her outside the cath lab. His name was Tosin Majekodunmi, and she had met him while accompanying her parents to their annual checkups at Euracare.

“My father liked him very much,” Adichie said. “I did come to consider him a friend. When my father died, he was very kind and called me.”

According to Adichie, Dr. Majekodunmi told her the doctors had saved Nkanu and he was now stable: “He said, ‘But everything is OK now because we got him back.’ And I kind of felt — I felt really confused.”

She shook her head and spoke more slowly, her voice thick with tears. “I trusted him,” she said.

Dr. Majekodunmi did not respond to interview requests from The Times.

The night Nkanu fell ill, she went home to gather the documents and payments necessary to transport him back to the United States the next morning in an air ambulance. She left and Esege stayed at the hospital.

Esege, who retired from his work as a family physician in Baltimore when the twins were born, was still at the hospital when he looked at the report the hospital’s staff had prepared for the air ambulance company. He was shocked to see that it said Nkanu’s pupils were fixed and dilated. And on the Blantyre coma scale the doctors had marked their son at zero in a range of one to five, meaning he had shown no eye movement and didn’t respond to pain.

Egese’s voice cracked as he described his reaction to me: “Nobody said anything to me about this. I mean, this basically means Nkanu is gone.”

Not dead yet, but lacking any meaningful brain function. Esege said he believed, based on the report, that Dr. Majekodunmi knew Nkanu was beyond saving after the first cardiac arrest, but he didn’t want to tell Adichie because of his closeness to her and her family.

Esege said the doctor had urged him not to call Adichie until the hospital could do a CT scan, but he replied that he couldn’t keep the information from her. He texted his wife and asked her to come back, and she returned around midnight. In the next few hours, Nkanu’s heart stopped at least two more times.

“So they basically are doing cardiac resuscitations on this poor boy for more than four hours, until 8 in the morning, when they decided to call it,” Egese said. “Nkanu, our son, was gone.”

It seemed that Esege’s theory about the timing of Nkanu’s death was not one he had shared with his wife. Adichie looked at him, incredulous, and asked, “So, sorry. We don’t actually know when our son died?”

She paused and then said again, in disbelief, “We don’t know when he died.”

Turning to me, Adichie said, “I’m actually hearing this for the first time. Some of it.” She then referred to Esege by his nickname. “I didn’t know about IV’s conversation with the doctor when I went home to try to get the payments for the ambulance. I think IV’s tried to protect me.”

Near us in the dining room, Nkanu’s highchair was still at the table, next to his brother’s. His clothes were still folded upstairs in his room. Adichie mentioned that she now had to buy clothes for one boy, not two, but was still in the habit of adding two of every item — T-shirt, shorts, sweater — to the online shopping cart.

Intermittently, throughout our conversation, she took out her phone and showed me videos of Nkanu. For brief moments, there were echoes of his laughter. On the screen of his mother’s phone, Nkanu sang and danced, played with her jewelry and climbed on Esege’s back while he pretended to be a horse, galloping the child across imaginary fields.

Not long after Nkanu died, Adichie and Esege filed a complaint with the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria — a separate entity from the one conducting the inquest — and in February the council announced an initial finding of negligence on the part of three physicians: Dr. Majekodunmi; Dr. Titus Ogundare, the anesthesiologist who sedated Nkanu; and a doctor from Atlantis Pediatric Hospital, where Nkanu was first treated. The three were suspended pending a formal hearing; the Atlantis physician has since been cleared.

Dr. Ogundare did not respond to requests for comment.

The coroner’s inquest itself has turned into a battle, with Adichie accusing Euracare of playing a “monstrous cynical game” by creating unnecessary delays. (The inquest has been delayed until the fall.) When Esege joined an inquest hearing remotely in June, Euracare shocked the couple by accusing them of a crime: destroying evidence by having their son cremated. According to local news reports, the hospital’s lawyer, Taiwo Osipitan, said: “What they did is punishable by 15 years imprisonment. The issue is whether somebody who has done something wrong under the law can push for an inquest.”

Sylvester Shih, Euracare’s chief operating officer, did not respond to a request for comment.

“I feel so bad for IV,” Adichie said. “He’s on Zoom. He’s hearing it all. He’s hearing when someone is saying that he destroyed evidence, and by evidence, they mean our child.”

Even before Nkanu’s death, Adichie and Esege were adjusting to the losses of both of her parents and Esege’s brother in recent years. She recalled a conversation she had with her husband on Jan. 7, the day after Nkanu died.

“I just remember looking at IV and saying, ‘Do we have to have another funeral?’ IV said, ‘I cannot.’ And IV said, ‘We’ll cremate him. We’ll take him with us because we can’t leave him behind.’”

Along with her four novels Adichie has given popular TED talks and published short fiction, essays, children’s literature and, after her father’s death in 2020, a book called “Notes on Grief.”

“When my father died, I was struck by the physicality of grief. And this time, even more so,” she told me. “I feel it. It’s in my stomach and it’s in my chest, and you’re just so tired every day. Everything is difficult. Everything. And then you have to pretend. You have to pretend because you have children, and you’re terrified of how they’re doing. Sometimes my son doesn’t want me to hold him because I’m so weepy. He’s 2. So I really try. It feels like the full manifestation of my grief is impossible because of the condition of being a mother.”

About then, the little boy woke up with a wail and Esege went upstairs to get him.

Later, he swept into the room, his sister’s sweater draped over his shoulders like a superhero’s cape. He crawled into the cradle of his mother’s lap until he saw that his father had a soccer ball and went tearing after it. It was the week of the World Cup semifinals and the family found the games to be an engaging distraction.

Then the front door opened and the couple’s daughter bounced in. Tall like her father, she was dressed in all pink, her favorite color. She whispered something to her mother and Adichie smiled. Monday is hamburger day and her daughter wanted to make sure that even though she had eaten a burger over the weekend, she would get to have her favorite American meal because it was still Monday.

When we talked, Adichie had not been back to the country of her birth, the place she has brought to life in novels beloved by millions of readers, in six months. She had mentioned that she and Esege were planning to return there soon, and I asked if they planned to take their son and daughter with them. They have taught their children to love Nigeria even as they learn about its structural and political challenges.

Adichie grimaced and said, “They’re the reason we’re going.”

“Really, we’ve had two homes forever,” she continued. “We were in Nigeria every Christmas, every Easter, every summer. Our daughter said to me recently, ‘Mama, Nigeria is my happy place.’ She’s the one who wants to go.’”

I asked what her little boy understood about all that had happened. She shook her head and said, “He always says his brother is in Lagos.”

Adichie said she had always loved Nigeria and felt grateful to have a home there and one in Maryland. She came to the United States at 19 to study at Drexel University in Philadelphia and went on to earn master’s degrees from Johns Hopkins and Yale.

“I think that America made it possible for me to write, which is my life’s vocation,” she said. “But Nigeria gave me everything I needed to be able to write. And I feel grateful for that.”

But is Nigeria still where she is supposed to be?

She wiped the tears from her face and continued: “I mean, it is so surreal, all of this. I still can’t believe we’re talking about my son who died. You’re going through something, but you also feel like you’re outside of it.”

After a moment she said softly, “I do not want to go back to Nigeria.”

I came to this story with some experience of having a child who needed intensive medical care. When I wrote to Adichie and Esege about an interview, I let them know that I was a journalist but also a mother who spent four months in the NICU with my child.A few weeks later, I traveled to their home in Baltimore where the couple sat together, it turns out for the first time, and went hour by hour through the last night of their son’s life.

Deborah Segun (b. 1994) is a multidisciplinary artist from Lagos, Nigeria, based in London.

item.title: Inside an Ancient Lebanese City Engulfed by War
item.description:
The ancient city of Tyre has come to embody the rhythms and brutality of war in southern Lebanon.

The city has been shaken by relentless Israeli bombardment, broken neighborhoods and endless funerals.

People have been driven from their homes to hospitals, shelters and, often, out of the city.

During lulls in the fighting, life seems to return to something close to normal, only for it to be shattered by renewed attacks.

By Abdi Latif Dahir

Visuals by Daniel Berehulak

Reporting from Tyre, Lebanon

Since early March, Tyre, located about 50 miles south of the capital, Beirut, has lived in the shadow of the war between Hezbollah, the Iran-backed armed group in Lebanon, and Israel. The war began days after the first U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.

For more than two months, reporters from The New York Times repeatedly returned to Tyre, as the city and its people endured a seemingly endless cycle of deadly strikes and tenuous cease-fires.

Services, including water and electricity, were frequently interrupted. People slept on the streets and along the beach, convinced that they would be safer in the open air than in their homes.

The city’s Christian quarter, largely spared in previous conflicts, was drawn into the fighting. In July, UNESCO added some of the city’s archaeological sites to its list of World Heritage sites in danger.

The war, though tempered by a precarious truce that was first signed in mid-April, has broadly devastated Lebanon, killing more than 4,380 people and displacing over a million, with Israel occupying large parts of the country’s south and destroying entire villages and neighborhoods. Israel has said that it wants to dismantle Hezbollah’s military infrastructure and prevent further attacks on Israeli communities near the Lebanese border.

For Rida Hijazi al-Dahab, the fighting in Tyre has exacted a devastating toll on his home, his business and nearly everything he owns. Minutes before the first cease-fire was set to go into effect, Israeli airstrikes flattened buildings in the residential block where his coffee shop was located. Israel said shortly afterward, without offering evidence, that its strikes over the previous 24 hours had targeted Hezbollah sites and personnel.

Mr. al-Dahab said he had been standing inside the cafe when the strikes hurled him against a wall and knocked him unconscious. He woke up to find that people were pulling him out of the debris from the building, which his grandfather had built decades ago.

“What did we do wrong to deserve this?” he asked in an interview in May.

On a recent evening, as the sun cast a golden glow over Tyre’s Mediterranean waterfront, water dripped from the cracked concrete where Mr. al-Dahab’s cafe once stood. Power lines hung low overhead and dust clung to the shattered walls as he looked over the scene of destruction. He said he had invested thousands of dollars into the business, money now lost.

“The candle of life has been switched off from this neighborhood,” Mr. al-Dahab said.

His neighborhood was not the only place that was shadowed by grief.

Across Tyre, death became part of the city’s daily rhythm. For weeks, the city was full of funerals, sometimes several in a single day.

For Lebanese Civil Defense emergency workers, who were hunkered down across the city and surrounding region, the toll was especially acute. Some were killed in so-called double-tap strikes, hit by the Israeli military as they rushed to treat or evacuate those killed or wounded from an initial strike, according to Lebanese health officials and human rights groups.

In many of those cases, Israel has said that its strikes were aimed at militants, without providing evidence. In some instances, it has said it is investigating the attacks.

More than 130 medical workers have been killed since the war began, according to Lebanon’s health ministry.

In Tyre, their funerals became scenes of collective mourning, with relatives leaning over coffins, scattering flowers and sharing memories of those they lost, sometimes as Israeli warplanes and drones roared overhead.

One of them was Hussein al-Sati, who was killed in April while he and his team responded to the scene of an Israeli strike. At his funeral, his 4-year-old daughter, Tala, praised her father for his bravery and called him a “hero.”

As the wailing grew louder and mourners crowded around the coffins, she broke down. Turning to her mother and relatives, she begged to return to Beirut.

“Let’s leave,” she cried.

As suddenly as the violence came, it would subside, and the city would find ways to slowly stitch itself back together.

Restaurants and cafes were always the first to reopen. They served shawarmas, matcha lattes and shisha as people looked out over the calm seafront, trying — if only for an afternoon — to pretend the war had paused. Fishermen returned to mend their boats and prepare for the next catch. Clothing stores reopened. The ice cream truck rolled back into town. Families came back, carrying little more than the bags they had fled with.

Vegetable markets reopened, too, their stalls still sparse. Traders like Bassam Nuwayri, 50, said they often had little to sell because farming across southern Lebanon had been devastated.

“We will always return here,” he said on a recent afternoon. “We have to remain steadfast on our land.”

Not everyone could return.

For many displaced residents, Tyre has become a place remembered rather than one to which they can return.

Zakia al-Or, 87, fled Tyre at the onset of the war in March. She is now staying with several family members in an old courthouse-turned-shelter in Sidon, a coastal city further north.

She spoke about following the man she loved to Tyre, raising her children there and perfecting generations-old family recipes. She stayed even after her children left for other parts of Lebanon and moved abroad, chasing work and escaping war.

Much of that life is gone. Her home was hit in the 2024 war between Hezbollah and Israel, she said, and then struck and damaged again in the most recent conflict.

Ms. al-Or described the emotional pain of losing pieces of her life over and over, and how, in old age, she had hoped for just a few peaceful years. She was in physical pain, too; her medications were running out, and she could barely sit up in bed.

She said she was ready to go anywhere — Beirut, Canada, the United States.

“The wars and the desperation never end,” she said. “This whole country is sad.”

That sadness is perhaps most visible in Tyre’s hospitals, where every strike has brought yet another patient, another family, another emergency.

For months, medical workers carried on with dwindling supplies as their own facilities came under attack. Inside, there was the child, wailing in pain from the shrapnel wounds that covered her body. The farmworker, who had lost both of her legs, her husband and several other family members in Israeli strikes. The nurses and doctors, sitting stunned amid shattered wards and offices, trying to make sense of what was left.

In June, a laboratory was damaged at Jabal Amel Hospital after an Israeli airstrike hit a nearby building.

A month earlier, a strike had hit a building near Hiram Hospital after the Israeli military ordered that it be evacuated, shattering windows and damaging parts of the hospital, including operating rooms, doctors said. At least four newborns were evacuated safely, according to the nursing supervisor, Mohammad Salem.

“We are scared,” Mr. Salem said.

For now, the rhythm of life is back in Tyre. It began to come back slowly, gingerly, after another fragile truce between Hezbollah and Israel was reached in June.

Along the shore, the Mediterranean rolls against the city. Some families have been reclaiming the pleasures of summer, gathering under colorful umbrellas, sharing meals and playing volleyball by the water. In the center of town, traders are slowly returning, rebuilding and repairing.

Shelling in the city’s outskirts — and across southern Lebanon — is still rattling the ground as drones hum overhead.

For residents like Mr. al-Dahab, the coffee shop owner, a semblance of ordinary life means reckoning with what happened while trying to find a way through the uncertainty ahead.

“I lost everything,” he said. But, he added, “It’s also a miracle that I am still alive.”

Sarah Chaayto and Hwaida Saad contributed reporting.

item.title: Walk This Way
item.description:
Fall is prime walking season: the cooling air, the changing colors. I have made a vow to take a good, substantial walk every day until hibernation season kicks in.

Sometimes I have to be creative to get myself out the door. So I’ve come up with some go-to themes for my walks. For example:

The Rage Walk. The other day, I was irked after I had been on hold with the I.R.S. for over an hour and laced up my sneakers. After I stomped around for a while, I eventually got distracted by my neighbor’s dahlias and found my anger had subsided. I make a point to take walks to savor happy feelings as well; on the recent news from my mom that her cancer is in remission, I took a peaceful, meandering morning stroll in a park near my house and listened to the birds sing.

The Melancholy Walk. Putting one foot in front of the other has been shown to reduce depression and anxiety. My daughter is headed to college next year, and I’m already glum about it. I find a nighttime stroll, looking up at the moon with Lana Del Rey in my earbuds, allows me to wallow a bit in feelings of loss, work through them a little, and maybe even see the beauty in some endings.

The Issue Walk. There’s something about perambulation that helps me work out my problems. My best friend and I have a ritual: If one of us is wrestling with some sort of dilemma, we’ll schedule a walk and hash it out. I’m in New Jersey and she’s in New York City, so we do it via earbuds. We’ll march along briskly, our walk providing a little forward momentum that makes us feel more confident and capable.

Sometimes I simply ask myself: Can I turn this activity into a walk? My boss and I have done our weekly check-in walking around the block outside the office. Next week I’ve scheduled a catch-up call with a former teacher who lives in another state, and I plan to do it while on the move. When I have time, I walk to the post office instead of driving.

I used to meet a friend I’ve known since the Clinton administration for regular lunch dates. After she canceled several times in a row, I (gently) asked what was up. She explained that money was tight and she just couldn’t swing eating out that much anymore.

So I proposed a walk instead. Our meandering walk-and-talks, it turns out, are much livelier than sitting in a restaurant. I’ve floated this idea to a few other friends in lieu of dates with price tags; no one has refused me yet.

Walking has been shown to lower risk for many types of cancer and heart disease. Research suggests it can ease lower back pain, and also build and maintain strong bones.

And if you’re seeking connection, a walk is a low-key way to put yourself out there and meet people. I’ve found that if someone has a dog or a young child, it’s particularly easy to strike up a chat.

When I encounter a pup, I might ask, “Is your dog usually this beautifully behaved?” Inevitably, the reply will be “God, no,” followed by a tale of mayhem.

I’ve found that toddlers crave power and respect; greeting them with “sir” or “madam” and a slight bow often thrills them. Or I might ask the child’s opinion on what I should have for my next meal (chicken nuggets and pizza are the front-runners).

I love that walking is accessible for all ages. I find I can extract more information from my teenager on a long ramble, and indeed there is research suggesting communication is easier when you’re walking side by side, with little eye contact, rather than face to face.

My father is 84 and likes to drop by my place for lunch. We used to sit in the kitchen and chat after eating. Now, I try to coax him outside for a stroll.

Last week, he resisted because it was rainy, so I told him I wouldn’t divulge a delicious piece of family gossip unless we did a few laps around the block.

Dad likes to pretend that he’s above gossip, but he’s not. His mouth pursed in disapproval, he stood up, put on his cap and headed for the door.

9/11 Anniversary

All four living ex-presidents gathered in Manhattan for a ceremony to mark the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks. President Trump spoke at the Pentagon.

Rudy Giuliani had called on Mayor Zohran Mamdani to skip the Manhattan memorial. But the two ended up shaking hands at the event. “I’ll pray for you,” Giuliani appeared to say. “It’s a really hard job.”

Trump, who has long railed against the so-called forever wars that followed 9/11, used his speech at the Pentagon ceremony to justify his military action in Iran.

Americans who enlisted in the military because of the attacks spoke about how that decision shaped their lives.

Chang W. Lee, a longtime Times photographer, captured an indelible image of that day: the collapse of the north tower. In the video below, he describes how he did it. Click to play.

Middle East

A drone attack launched from Iraqi territory caused Saudi Arabia to shut down a critical oil pipeline. The global price of oil briefly jumped to about $110 a barrel, and ended Friday under $105.

The Houthi militia seized a strategic island in the Red Sea after days of fierce fighting, giving Iran sway over another crucial oil route.

“These waters aren’t safe”: Gulf tankers are running out of ways to ship oil.

Other Big Stories

The contractor that renovated the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool blamed its own errors, not vandals, for the pool’s peeling liner.

The crew of a fishing vessel rescued a 15-year-old Alaskan boy whose overturned boat had been drifting for days in the Bering Sea. Two of the boy’s relatives died.

Film and TV

“Practical Magic 2,” which arrives nearly three decades after the original, stars Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman as sisters with a romantic curse. It is “precisely what I expected it to be,” our critic writes. (She means it as a compliment.)

In a charming and often moving new documentary, the director Sam Green profiles a series of people, mostly women, who were at one time the oldest person in the world.

Does your kid need a brain break after a busy week of school? Here are five children’s movies you can stream today.

Music

Nashville International Airport is set to be renamed in memory of Dolly Parton.

In Beck’s new album, “Ride Lonesome,” he returns to a more basic sound: a guy, a guitar and a broken heart.

Sara Bareilles, the singer-songwriter who became a theater fan favorite with her musical “Waitress,” airs her recent anguishes on “Good Grief,” her first studio album in seven years.

More Culture

A landmark retrospective of Yayoi Kusama in Amsterdam, the last she worked on before her recent death, is a worthy showcase for her vast and varied oeuvre, our critic writes.

Julia Roberts will return to Broadway early next year in an all-star production of “Small Mouth Sounds,” an experimental comedic play about a silent retreat.

The U.S. Open finals: Could this finally be the year? Ben Shelton will have the crowd in Flushing, Queens, behind him tomorrow as he looks to become the first American man in 23 years to win the country’s premier tennis tournament. Of course, it won’t be easy to get past Alexander Zverev, who has been surging ever since he won the French Open in June.

On the women’s side, today’s final will be a blockbuster showdown between the world’s new No. 1 ranked player (Elena Rybakina) and the two-time defending champion (Aryna Sabalenka). It starts at 4 p.m. Eastern.

By Melissa Clark

This weekend is Rosh Hashana, the Jewish New Year, when apples and honey are traditional parts of the menu. For something a little different, why not try David Tanis’s recipe for an easy apple tart, made with phyllo dough, marmalade and gently spiced apples? He drizzles it all with a bit of honey right before serving. To make it slightly richer, substitute puff pastry for the phyllo. Either way, it will be a glossy, golden finish to your meal.

The Hunt: These newlyweds agreed about everything, except when to move. Which Washington, D.C., home did they pick? Play our game.

What you get for $375,000: A cottage in Brunswick, Ga.; a Victorian in Columbus, Ind.; and a Spanish-style home in San Antonio.

Real or A.I.? Virtually staged homes have become so pervasive that some states and cities are requiring real estate agents to disclose when they use A.I. to significantly alter listings.

Blending in: A landscape designer collaborated with family members on a weekend house in Spain where building and garden seem to “melt into each other.”

The “Wave House”: Two architects set about restoring a distinctive midcentury modern house in Lambertville, N.J., to its original glory. See inside.

Regularly getting that dreaded “Storage Full” notification? You don’t necessarily need to pay for more cloud storage. Instead, spend 10 to 15 minutes each month freeing up space. Start by deleting any apps you no longer want or need; your settings menu can make this process easier by pulling up your least-used apps. Photos and videos eat up tons of space, so delete any unnecessary duplicates, screenshots or screen recordings. Consider setting your text messages to auto-delete after a designated amount of time. And, finally, remove any downloads (say, of TV shows or podcast episodes) that you’ve already streamed or know you’ll never get around to. — Brenda Stolyar

item.title: Why Carney Isn’t Rushing Back to the Negotiating Table
item.description:
If nothing else, the trade war President Trump started against Canada last year feels relentless.

Below, you can find all of our trade articles from the past week — and there are a number of them. But let’s recap what’s transpired and look at where all of this may be headed.

On Tuesday, Canada struck back against the United States: Tariffs of 15, 25 and 50 percent took effect that morning on about $20 billion a year of American exports. The move was Prime Minister Mark Carney’s answer to the 50 percent tariffs Mr. Trump imposed after trade talks between the two countries collapsed last month.

[Read: Brushing Aside Trump’s Threats, Canada Retaliates on Tariffs]

That was just the start. Mr. Trump first threatened to close the U.S. market to business jets made in Quebec and Ontario by Bombardier. At another point, he floated blocking all trade with Canada and other countries running a trade surplus in goods with the United States.

He ultimately didn’t go that far. (Mr. Trump’s 50 percent tariffs were themselves partly retaliation for tariffs Canada imposed last year, after Mr. Trump placed levies of up to 50 percent on Canadian steel, aluminum and autos — a move that violated the free trade agreement between the two countries and Mexico.)

But he did move to shut the border to a range of Canadian products. All Canadian beer, wine and liquor top the list. Whey, the liquid left over from cheese and yogurt production, has also lost the U.S. market. Dairies once dumped it into rivers and lakes, fueling algae blooms, but it is now in demand for protein supplements. Mr. Trump also targeted the founding family of Bombardier, which still controls the aerospace company, banning the three-wheeled motorcycles made by another of its Quebec-based companies.

[Read: Trump Announces Ban on Some Canadian Imports]

Tit and tat have been busy. And few people anticipate the back and forth between the two former economic allies to end soon.

[Read: Carney, at a Cabinet Retreat, Considers Further Trade Strikes Against the U.S.]

Unlike Mr. Tump’s reflex to act quickly, Canada appears to be biding its time. Mr. Carney and his cabinet spent most of the week emphasizing efforts to build closer ties with other nations and plans for domestic infrastructure spending, avoiding questions about further retaliation.

Polls show strong support for Mr. Carney’s decision to walk away from a bad deal with the United States and retaliate. Many Canadians would like to go further, favoring export taxes to raise the price of oil, gas and electricity headed to the United States.

I spoke this week with Andrew McDougall, an assistant professor of Canadian politics at the University of Toronto. He said the national mood against compromise had put Mr. Carney in a bind on reopening talks.

Since negotiations collapsed, Mr. Carney and his officials have said the failure stemmed from several U.S. demands. Those included tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos that would have stayed too high for those industries to compete; a broader expectation that Canada accept tariffs from a country with which it has a free-trade agreement; changes to Canadian laws protecting the country’s culture and French language; and a demand that Canada align with Mr. Trump’s trade policies rather than pursue deals with other countries.

All of it, Mr. Carney has said, is a nonstarter.

American officials have disputed parts of that account, but they continue to make it clear that Mr. Trump will not exempt any nation from tariffs.

“The politics of this is difficult,” Professor McDougall said, adding that Mr. Carney “has to be seen to be standing up for the country.”

“It’s a difficult moment to talk about trade talks when it’s not clear where those will go or what those will look like,” he said.

Much of Mr. Carney’s public support, in Professor McDougall’s view, reflects a perception that he is “acting reasonably,” a dramatic contrast with how Canadians view Mr. Trump.

“It’s that reasonable approach that I think Canadians are responding to, and I think that’s part of the reason why he’s proved as popular as he has,” Professor McDougall said. “It doesn’t look like there’s much of a political appetite to restart these things, given that Carney seems to have the public behind him. I think he’s content to sort of leave it at that for right now.”

item.title: The Doctor Pressuring African Leaders to Own the Ebola Response
item.description:
The rumba band paused for a moment as the presidents of the Democratic Republic of Congo and South Africa walked down a red carpet together to lunch in a garden pavilion in Congo’s presidential residence.

Watching with satisfaction a few yards away was Dr. Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, known as the Africa C.D.C. A Congolese physician with a punishing work ethic, a PowerPoint presentation for seemingly every occasion and a taste for shirts embroidered with his own name, he had convened the presidents to discuss the Ebola epidemic, which so far has killed more than 3,300 people in eastern Congo.

On a continent long accustomed to Western agencies and foreign donors driving emergency responses, Dr. Kaseya is pushing for a major shift — one made increasingly urgent by shrinking Western aid budgets. Jetting around Africa, he is pushing the continent’s presidents to take financial and political ownership of public health. He says it is a question of African sovereignty.

“This response is led in Africa by Africans, for Africans, with support from our partners,” he told the two presidents — and some of those Western “partners,” or donors — at a meeting after the fancy lunch in July. “It’s not the reverse.”

The devastating 2014 Ebola outbreak in West Africa convinced the African Union that the continent urgently needed its own C.D.C. It was launched in 2017. Dr. Kaseya, who took office in 2023, is only the second person to hold the leadership position.

His leadership has split opinion in global health circles. To supporters, he has a clear vision for the continent and the ability to see it through, and he has elevated the Africa C.D.C. into a formidable political force.

To critics, his tenure has been turbulent and his style abrasive. According to investigative reporting last year by Devex, a news outlet covering global development, extravagant spending on travel and meetings has raised some funders’ concerns, and some donors no longer want to work with the Africa C.D.C. because of Dr. Kaseya’s leadership. Dr. Kaseya said that in response to some of the earlier Devex reporting, he launched institutional reviews that ultimately did not substantiate its accusations.

As proof of his success, he pointed to the Africa C.D.C.’s rapid growth in funding and spending; 12 recent audits, with all problems resolved on schedule; and an official African Union evaluation this year that recently rated his performance as “Outstanding.”

But there has been turmoil on his staff.

This year, Dr. Kaseya ordered three of the agency’s five regional directors, whom he had appointed, back to headquarters, saying they had been rejected by their host countries. They fought the decision, complaining to an African Union tribunal, which ordered them reinstated. The standoff ended in July when a top African Union official backed Dr. Kaseya and recalled the directors.

Still, trust in his leadership appears to be building. The World Bank, for example, upgraded one of its rankings of the agency from “moderately unsatisfactory” two years ago to “satisfactory” last year. Observers have described several of his recent hires as impressive.

In an interview in his hotel suite in Kinshasa, Congo’s capital city, Dr. Kaseya acknowledged that he has a “strong personality” and does not tolerate weakness or “misbehavior” on his staff.

“If I find any kind of misbehavior, I’ll help you to be out of the organization,” he said.

Dr. Kaseya, 55, said that his mother, a nurse in a Kinshasa hospital, inspired his medical career. He described how at age 6 or 7, he saw a 1-year-old die of measles, and watched his mother weep because she could not save the child.

“Me, I need to save life,” he remembered telling her. “I will become a nurse.” Her reply, he said: “You can even become more than that. You can become a doctor.”

And so, he resolved to be a doctor — until, at 15, his ambitions turned to music. After watching a performance by the Congolese rumba star and international heartthrob Koffi Olomide, he said, he approached the singer and told him he wanted to be a musician. “OK, sing,” he recalled Mr. Olomide saying. After the impromptu audition, Mr. Olomide told him to stick to medicine.

“You see how he managed to kill my passion,” Dr. Kaseya said, smiling on the hotel sofa as night deepened and his staff brought him takeout for dinner.

Working late at night is imperative because that is when you talk to presidents on the phone, he said. He wakes every morning at 3 to have an hour to himself to think, he said, before launching into the workday. He and his team said he broke only to spend an hour or two every evening cooking Congolese dishes.

Dr. Kaseya’s wife and daughters are in Canada, so they have no claim on his time. While on the two-day trip to Kinshasa, he wanted to visit his mother, but said he could not break away.

The many pictures of him with politicians posted on social media have earned him some side eye. For Dr. Kaseya, though, playing the role of a high-level diplomat is key to getting the Africa C.D.C. respected — and funded by African governments.

He picked up his phone and opened his contacts. “If I just put ‘president’ here, you’ll see a number of them are connected with me by WhatsApp. At least 40. I’m talking to them directly.”

Dr. Kaseya has built on the work of John Nkengasong, who established the Africa C.D.C.’s credibility during the Covid-19 pandemic and leveraged it into greater autonomy from the African Union.

Dr. Yodi Alakija, a prominent global health leader, said it was long past time Africa had power over its own public health. Global health organizations failed Africa during the pandemic, she said, and would do so again because many were built during colonialism, with colonial aims.

“If we don’t look after ourselves, the world will leave us behind,” she said.

But only 21 percent of the agency’s funding comes from African governments, Dr. Kaseya said, leaving it reliant on foundations and other donors.

Dr. Boghuma Titanji, a Cameroonian physician and infectious diseases expert, said, “You cannot claim to have ownership and sovereignty of every decision you’re making when still there is a funding gap, and you’re relying on external funders who are still going to dictate to some degree the agenda that you’re able to pursue.” This, she said, put the organization in a “fragile and vulnerable situation.”

In the interview, Dr. Kaseya said changing this paradigm was a major focus. He described making Congo confirm how much money it would provide for the Ebola response before he would approach donors for funds, arguing that it was primarily Congo’s responsibility.

In the meeting with the Congolese president, Félix Tshisekedi, and the South African president, Cyril Ramaphosa, in July, Dr. Kaseya said he was “so proud” of them for their countries’ financing — $50 million from Congo and $13.5 million from South Africa.

Later, he said that $90 million of the $120 million African countries had promised for the response had been disbursed so far. “This is amazing, from African countries,” he said.

Paying for its own public health is one way for Africa to take charge of its own future, he said — an exhortation he said he frequently heard from African presidents.

“You know, sometimes to have a broad vision implemented, we need to look for entry points,” he said. “And health is a major entry point today.”

His own “broad vision” for the Africa C.D.C. appears to encompass much more than public health. He wants to use the immediate Ebola crisis to solve longer-running problems in the affected area of eastern Congo, and send home many of the hundreds of thousands of people living in camps there. That would stamp out cholera and bolster the economy, as well as stop Ebola, he argues.

To achieve this, Dr. Kaseya nearly tripled the amount of money he said the Ebola response plan needed, from $518 million to $1.4 billion.

Some global health veterans accuse him of adding unrealistic responsibilities to Africa C.D.C.’s plate. He acknowledged that managing displaced populations is not part of the agency’s mandate, but that he sees a role for it in lobbying and raising funds for humanitarian work.

“There is a category of people who still think that Africans are not hard workers,” he said. “I will not fight with them, but I will show them.”

item.title: Why Mokha, Historic Port That Shaped the Coffee Trade, Is a Prize in Yemen’s War
item.description:
Long before it was captured by Houthi forces this week in Yemen’s civil war, the centuries-old Red Sea port of Mokha was famed as one of the original gateways of the global coffee trade.

At its height, from the 16th to 18th centuries, the city was a wealthy hub of merchants and coffee houses in a region that oversaw a monopoly on the world’s coffee bean supply for more than a hundred years. That legacy stretches into modern coffee culture, with the city giving its name to coffee beans, specialty products and the mocha, a chocolate and espresso drink.

Some of the traits that allowed Mokha to dominate the coffee trade centuries ago have also made it a strategic — and coveted — prize in the current conflict in Yemen.

Mokha’s proximity to the Bab el-Mandab Strait, a narrow waterway about 50 miles south of the city that links the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean, has for centuries given it leverage over one of the world’s most important trade corridors.

Here’s a look at the city’s history.

The Ottoman Turks occupied Yemen in the late 1530s, and transformed Mokha from a small fishing village into a coffee superpower.

Coffee already had a foothold in the region. About a century earlier, scholars believe, people there were the first to consume a drink that modern coffee drinkers would recognize. The practice may have started with Arab Sufi monks, who drank the stimulating beverage to stay awake for midnight prayers. By the mid-1500s, coffee drinking had become widespread in the area, which saw a number of other coffee firsts.

“Yemen is the home not only of the social habit of drinking coffee as the beverage that we know today, it’s also the home of large-scale coffee cultivation and really the first purveyor of coffee to the world,” said Nancy Um, the author of “The Merchant Houses of Mocha,” about the city’s trade history.

In Yemen, the Turks began cultivating coffee on a commercial scale in the highlands around Mokha and exported it throughout their empire.

They also established a monopoly, banning coffee beans from leaving Yemen unless they were first boiled or roasted to prevent germination, wrote Mark Pendergrast in his 1999 book, “Uncommon Grounds.” (According to Mr. Pendergrast, in the 1600s, a Muslim pilgrim named Baba Budan smuggled seven seeds out by strapping them to his stomach and later successfully cultivated the plants in India, although scholars debate the story’s veracity.)

Mokha’s proximity to the Bab el-Mandab Strait was central to its rise, connecting it to the Mediterranean through the Red Sea, and to Asia through the Indian Ocean. Today, ships must pass the strait to reach the Suez Canal and European waters beyond.

Mokha’s population of multiethnic and multifaith traders moved products including metals, textiles and spices, but it became heavily associated with coffee in the 17th century, when major European trading houses, including the East India Companies of England and the Netherlands, set up shop there.

“They consolidated the association between Mocha and coffee by labeling all of the beans that they purchased in Yemen and shipped from the port of Mokha as ‘Mokha coffee,’” Ms. Um said.

By the 1720s, however, coffee was being cultivated in the Caribbean and in Java, Indonesia, and Mokha’s central role diminished. Its death knell came in the early 1800s when the British took Aden, a port city to the east, and made it their main trade hub in the region, Ms. Um said.

A modern port was established in Mokha in the 1950s, but by then the region’s coffee industry had mostly disappeared.

Over the years, Yemen has converted much of its farmable land to the production of khat, a plant chewed for its amphetaminelike effects. That includes the country’s coffee-producing regions, which are largely under Houthi control.

“When coffee was replaced, it kind of doomed Yemen,” said Ibrahim Al-Marashi, an associate professor of Middle East history at California State University.

Mr. Al-Marashi said that khat, which is sold and consumed locally, is a drain on household savings and a drag on the economy. It is also water intensive, he said, giving more power to the Houthis, who control key water supplies in some areas.

In recent years, however, there has been a movement to reestablish the coffee industry in Mokha and Yemen, and to connect local farmers to Yemeni coffee shops around the world.

“Farmers are now seeing coffee as a potential alternative to khat and a way to uplift themselves,” said Mokhtar Alkhanshali, who owns a coffee business in Yemen that connects around 6,000 farmers to international roasters.

The recent-flare up of the conflict in Yemen, however, has jeopardized recent gains, he said. It has put farmers in physical danger, made it harder for them to export their products and threatened to push them back to khat, Mr. Alkhanshali said.

“For the first time in years, coffee was giving Yemenis something to hope for,” he said. “Now the port that should be shipping that coffee to the world is a battlefield.”

item.title: As Oil Prices Rise, BRICS Leaders Have What U.S. Doesn’t: Iran at the Table
item.description:
The summit of the BRICS group of emerging economies is designed to show what world leadership looks like when the West is not in the room.

And as widening clashes in the Middle East send global energy prices soaring, the gathering in New Delhi this weekend gives the leaders of China, India and Russia something Washington does not have: a seat at the table with Iran.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India is hosting the BRICS club — named after its earliest members, Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — that has been conceived as a counterweight to the West.

The Indian capital has largely been shut down for the meeting. Soldiers in khaki uniforms carrying rifles patrolled the streets, and steel road blocks cluttered the city center. Highways leading from the airport were also blanketed with BRICS signs depicting Mr. Modi alongside slogans such as: “Together we build, together we rise.”

That slogan points to the hope that the BRICS group has of projecting solidarity among its membership, which has expanded in recent years to include countries such as Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates and Indonesia. The message of unity stands in contrast to the global friction emanating from the Trump administration’s tariffs and the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, which has disrupted global energy corridors.

In reality, expectations are low that BRICS, a loose bloc, will be able to step up to fill that gap in leadership, let alone broker a diplomatic off-ramp to the crisis in the Middle East.

The group has been split by tensions between Iran and the United Arab Emirates, a U.S. security partner that has been targeted by thousands of Iranian ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones since the war started in February. Divisions prevented the group from producing a joint statement in May after a meeting of BRICS foreign ministers. (The U.A.E. sent Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the crown prince of Abu Dhabi, who arrived on Friday.)

“The world is really rapidly fracturing, and in theory that’s really kind of what the BRICS have been saying all along,” said Alexander Gabuev, director of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin. “But they’re really wildly underperforming.”

“It’s very difficult to have such a big and expanded club of countries that are united by their animosity to Western hegemony but have very different interests, sometimes opposing each other, sometimes at war with each other,” he added.

Both President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and President Masoud Pezeshkian of Iran, whose countries are mired in wars and under fierce pressure from the West in the form of sanctions, moved quickly on Friday to press their agendas even before the summit started.

Mr. Pezeshkian criticized U.S. power and urged fellow members to build alternative financial tools to protect themselves from Western pressure. “Who said it should decide for the entire world, that others have no rights, and that whatever they want everyone else has to obey?” he said in a speech. “This is something we will not accept.”

Mr. Modi, however, used a meeting with Mr. Pezeshkian on Friday to deliver a pointed message, urging him to safeguard “freedom of navigation and commerce” — a tacit reference to the chokeholds on the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea that threaten India’s own fuel imports.

That messaging is the kind of global leadership that Mr. Modi wants to be seen exercising. He does not share the same opposition to the West as Mr. Putin and Mr. Pezeshkian, embodying instead India’s historical preference for nonalignment and strategic friendships with powers from across the ideological spectrum. India’s chief rival for influence in the group is China, which has sought to use BRICS to displace U.S. power.

The summit is an opportunity for Mr. Modi to burnish his statesman credentials at a time when his political power at home has weakened and the Indian economy continues to take a back seat to China’s.

The Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, arrived for the summit on Saturday, but officials have not said if he will meet with Mr. Pezeshkian.

Iran is Beijing’s closest strategic partner in the Middle East, but China also has economic ties with Persian Gulf states that have been targeted by Iranian strikes.

At a recent regional security summit in Kyrgyzstan, Mr. Xi and Mr. Pezeshkian met only briefly on the sidelines rather than in a separate bilateral meeting.

That fueled speculation that Beijing was unhappy over the war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Mr. Xi could have also been distancing himself from Tehran to avoid provoking President Trump, whom he is scheduled to meet in Washington later this month.

“A substantive bilateral meeting in New Delhi would therefore carry significance well beyond protocol,” said Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group.

“It could help clarify whether China still sees Iran as a strategic partner worth investing political capital in at a moment of acute pressure, or whether Beijing is increasingly keeping Tehran at arm’s length,” Mr. Azizi said.

Perhaps more important to China is Mr. Xi’s meeting with Mr. Modi later in the day.

Mr. Xi’s visit is the first he has made to India in seven years, and is a sign of the continued stabilization of relations between Beijing and New Delhi. Ties hit a low in 2020 following a clash of Indian and Chinese forces in a disputed border region.

Other leaders arriving in New Delhi brought their own awkward entanglements with the group’s Western-skeptic tilt.

President Cyril Ramaphosa of South Africa shares Mr. Modi’s preference for using BRICS to build relationships across the globe. But the coalition has also created diplomatic headaches for Pretoria.

In January, South Africa was criticized by the Trump administration for allowing Iran to participate in BRICS naval drills off the South African coast at a time when the Iranian government faced accusations of fatally crushing street protests in Iran.

Mr. Ramaphosa said that China was running the exercises and that South African waters were chosen because of the convenient location.

South African officials have been disappointed that the bloc has not been able to reach consensus opinions on divisive conflicts like the wars in Iran and Gaza, said David Africa, an international relations analyst based in Cape Town.

“South Africa has knocked its head and realizes it won’t extract much diplomatically on the issues it’s concerned about,” Mr. Africa said. Instead, he said, South Africa is likely to focus on economic issues like trade, business and development at the summit.

One of the BRICS group’s most ambitious economic goals is to reduce global reliance on the dollar.

“De-dollarization,” as the effort is known, would throw a lifeline to countries like Russia and Iran, which have struggled to pay for imported goods since the United States and other Western countries restricted their access to the dollar.

The dollar’s status as the world’s reserve currency is an “exorbitant privilege” for the United States, economists say — and it’s a privilege that Mr. Trump intends to keep. At the start of his second term, he wrote that any country trying to “create a new BRICS Currency” to circumvent the dollar could “say goodbye to selling into the beautiful U.S. economy.”

An alternative reserve currency is not realistic at this point. But many countries that benefit from having the dollar as the world’s standard legal tender — India, for instance, which fears a financial future dominated by China — still want to see its dominance decrease. India has proposed that BRICS countries should link their banking systems more directly, allowing them to pay debts to one another without converting sums into dollars.

It is already buying oil from Russia using rupees and rubles.

Reporting was contributed by Valerie Hopkins in Moscow, Rania Khaled in Cairo, John Eligon in Johannesburg and Yeganeh Torbati in Istanbul.

item.title: Music Stars Are Dragged Into South Africa’s Immigration Controversy
item.description:
The South African singer Tyla canceled a performance in Nigeria after protests. The amapiano star Musa Keys, also South African, was removed from a festival lineup in Zimbabwe. And Salif Keïta, a revered musician from Mali, canceled a show in South Africa over what he called “xenophobic violence.”

As anti-immigrant fervor swells across South Africa, artists and fans are beginning to speak out, demanding that the country address the wave of threats and violence that has caused thousands of people to flee the continent’s largest economy.

African heads of state have condemned South Africa and called on the African Union to hold the country accountable. Nigeria is demanding that South Africa compensate citizens who fled their homes and were repatriated. South Africa recently lost an important continentwide leadership role dealing with telecommunications, and some say it was because of the country’s damaged diplomatic standing.

And now the country’s musicians and entertainers are facing backlash, too.

“It’s about coming together as a people and saying, ‘No, we have a voice, and that voice matters,’” said Solomon Buchi, a Nigerian writer and commentator who was among those who took to social media to protest the Tyla concert in Lagos.

Gayton McKenzie, the South African government minister overseeing arts and culture, rejected the idea that South Africans were xenophobic and that the country’s artists should be blamed. The South African government says it targets illegal immigration and is focused on protecting the country’s borders.

“Enforcing immigration law is not xenophobia,” said Mr. McKenzie, who campaigned largely on an anti-immigration platform and who helped popularize the slogan “Abahambe” (meaning “let them go” in Zulu), which is chanted at many anti-immigrant protests.

The wave of anti-immigrant sentiment that has swept across the country includes vigilante groups raiding immigrant communities and taking it upon themselves to kick them out of the country.

The violence and heated rhetoric have made many foreigners leave South Africa. At least 86,000 foreign nationals have been deported or repatriated from mid-June to late August, according to the South African government.

Mr. Keïta, the Malian artist, said in a Facebook post that he could not “ignore the reports of xenophobic violence against our African brothers and sisters.” His manager, Carolina Vallejo, confirmed his decision.

Mr. Keïta, 77, has been a mainstay of South African jazz and cultural festivals. His ties to South Africa stretch back decades, including a performance at the Nelson Mandela 70th birthday tribute concert at Wembley Stadium in 1988, an event linked to the international anti-apartheid movement.

He stressed that his decision not to perform in South Africa was not a rejection of South Africans. “To be clear — I am not closing the door on South Africa,” he wrote. “I am closing the door on violence.”

Tyla, a Grammy Award winner, has built a significant following in Nigeria and has worked with some of the country’s biggest stars, including Ayra Starr, Tems and Wizkid. But Nigerians criticized her scheduled appearance in Lagos, accusing her of staying silent instead of using her platform to condemn the anti-immigrant attacks.

Tyla has not publicly commented on why her Lagos concert was canceled, and her representatives did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Blessing Jake spent months organizing a music festival in Zimbabwe when, in July, he began seeing social media posts with people threatening to boycott the event if South African artists were not removed from the lineup.

The Buddie Beats Concert was scheduled to take place at Victoria Falls, and Mr. Jake had worked for months to secure the concert’s biggest acts, including Mafikizolo, a South African band.

In the end, Mr. Jake removed Mafikizolo from the bill. He said he lost hundreds of thousands of dollars as a result. Mr. Jake said he hoped the negative climate around South African artists could be resolved quickly.

“Business-wise,” he said, “xenophobia is very expensive.”

item.title: U.S. and Brazil Partnered in Fighting Crime. A Diplomatic Spat Threatens That.
item.description:
A diplomatic rift is hindering cooperation between the United States and Brazil on jointly fighting organized crime, according to U.S. and Brazilian officials, an issue the Trump administration has placed at the center of its agenda in the Western Hemisphere.

The State Department is withholding visas for two Brazilian federal police agents assigned to posts in the United States, where they would be working with U.S. Homeland Security Investigations and other federal agencies to combat transnational crimes, according to one American and three senior Brazilian officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

In response, Brazil is now also blocking the visa of a U.S. law enforcement official meant to be stationed in the country, according to the American and Brazilian officials.

The U.S. government, citing a busy agenda, also declined a request for a visit by Brazilian customs and revenue agents investigating money laundering and arms smuggling by international drug gangs, according to two other Brazilian officials.

Brazil and the United States have a long history of jointly investigating international crimes, like fraud and trafficking, and sending law enforcement officials to each other’s countries. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has had an attaché in Brazil for over two decades.

In the past, joint action by Brazil and the United States has helped the authorities dismantle international corruption schemes, piracy networks and human trafficking rings.

That type of close cooperation, experts say, is becoming crucial for fighting Latin America’s drug gangs, which have more resources and greater geographic reach than ever before.

“Today, criminal factions know no borders,” said Edvandir Felix de Paiva, the president of Brazil’s association of federal police commissioners. “So we need to be working together.”

The recent disruptions in cooperation, which have not been previously reported, come against a backdrop of strained relations over the past year, stemming from President Trump’s attempts to meddle in Brazil’s internal affairs. This rift has only deepened in recent months with the administration’s apparent readiness to help Flávio Bolsonaro, the right-wing candidate challenging President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a leftist, in Brazil’s elections in October.

Fighting transnational gangs has become a top priority for the Trump administration, and, in that fight, it has joined forces with Latin American countries led by conservative leaders. But fraying diplomatic ties may be derailing cooperation between the United States and Brazil, the Western Hemisphere’s most populous nations.

“The perception is that U.S. security policy toward Brazil has become entangled in politics,” said Robert Muggah, a security expert and research director of the Igarapé Institute, a Brazil-based research institution. “It hasn’t led to a fundamental rupture,” he added, “but it has introduced new complexities into the relationship and shaded it with levels of mistrust.”

The State Department declined to comment on the specifics of the visas, but said in a statement that the Trump administration was protecting “the nation and its citizens by upholding the highest standards of national security and public safety through our visa process.” The department added that it would continue working with Brazil to advance “longstanding shared interests.”

The U.S. Customs and Border Protection said in a statement it was committed to engaging with Brazilian authorities to advance “security goals and disrupt transnational crime.”

Brazil’s federal police and Foreign Ministry declined to comment. The Finance Ministry, which oversees the nation’s customs, revenue and border control agency, said the two nations maintain a dialogue aimed at exchanging best practices and combating transnational crime.

The two Brazilian federal police agents who have not been granted visas were scheduled to take their posts in Miami and New York last month, according to the Brazilian officials. They had already been selected and vetted by U.S. and Brazilian authorities early this year as part of a routine personnel change, one of the officials said.

One of the federal police attachés was to replace Marcelo Ivo de Carvalho, who was expelled from the United States in April and accused by the Trump administration of a “political witch hunt” over his role in the arrest of a former Brazilian intelligence chief. The chief ​had fled to the United States after he was convicted of plotting a coup in his home country with the former President Jair Bolsonaro.

The elder Mr. Bolsonaro, an ally of Mr. Trump’s, is serving a 27-year sentence over his attempt to cling to power. In response to Mr. Carvalho’s expulsion, Brazil revoked the credentials of a U.S. law enforcement agent working in Brasília, the capital.

In another reciprocal move, Brazil is now withholding a visa for the U.S. law enforcement agent’s successor until its own police attachés are allowed to take up their U.S. posts, according to two senior Brazilian officials. The authorities in both countries are still in negotiations over the visas, American and Brazilian officials said.

A team of nearly a dozen agents from Brazil’s customs and revenue agency also asked to visit their U.S. counterparts in Washington in June, as part of a recent push to increase cooperation in countering transnational money laundering and smuggling operations. But U.S. authorities declined their request, citing a crowded agenda through November, the two Brazilian officials said.

Under a new intelligence-sharing system introduced this year, customs agents in each country were alerting each other about suspicious container shipments, helping U.S. and Brazilian authorities to intercept illicit cargo, such as weapons, according to one of the officials.

While police and intelligence experts say this kind of technical cooperation between Brazil and the United States continues, a lack of high-level coordination may thwart more ambitious plans.

While Brazil does not export significant quantities of drugs to the United States, it is a major transit route for cocaine heading to Europe, Africa and elsewhere. Brazilian gangs are also increasingly forging alliances with Mexican and Colombian gangs and finding new ways to smuggle drugs out of Latin America.

Experts say Brazilian organized criminal groups use the U.S. banking system to launder profits from illicit activities. The United States is also a key source for these groups of illegal arms, smuggled from U.S. states with permissive gun laws. Last month, Brazilian police arrested two men in connection with weapons parts mailed from Florida.

During multiple meetings and phone calls over the past year, including as recently as Aug. 21, Mr. Lula has pitched Mr. Trump on closer cooperation on combating organized crime.

At a White House meeting in May, Mr. Lula delivered a proposal on how the two countries could fight drug gangs together by targeting their weapons and finances, according to a Brazilian official. The Trump administration never responded to the proposal, the official said.

That same month, the United States moved to designate the country’s two largest drug gangs as terrorist organizations after aggressive lobbying by Mr. Bolsonaro and his allies, who have accused Mr. Lula of being weak on crime. Public security is a major concern for many Brazilians and a key issue in October’s presidential election.

The full effect of the U.S. designation is not yet clear, but it has already led to at least one policing stumble. The United States used the designation to apply sanctions to people who had secretly been under investigation by Brazilian police, revealing their links to gangs and tipping them off to the probe. As a result, Brazilian police had to rush to arrest the targets.

At the same time, Washington has sought to strengthen cooperation with conservative leaders in the Western Hemisphere through the Shield of the Americas, a new security alliance against drug traffickers that does not include Brazil. Some members, including Ecuador and Colombia, have agreed to joint military operations with the United States in their countries.

Last month, Brazil was also not invited to a U.S.-led gathering of security officials from Latin America and the Caribbean at the United Nations.

The diplomatic scuffle between Brazil and the United States escalated in recent months, with a series of other visa rejections and cancellations. But while the Trump administration has sought to use visas as part of its effort to assert its dominance in Latin America, this approach may only further alienate Brazil.

“We want to have Brazil closer to the United States — not further away,” said Jimmy Story, a former U.S. ambassador and a founding partner of Global Frontier Advisors, a consulting firm. “And this kind of diplomacy has the opposite effect.”

Alice Maciel and Thayz Guimarães contributed reporting from Brasília.

item.title: ‘We Left in the Clothes We Were Wearing’: Yemenis Flee New Fighting
item.description:
At least half of the population is hungry. Millions of children are unvaccinated. A measles outbreak is spreading.

The people of Yemen have survived the indignities of a more than decade-long civil war. This past week, many were again running for their lives.

A new round of fighting has erupted between the Houthis, the Iran-backed militia in the north, and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government, widening the regional conflict that began early this year with the U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran.

More than 46,000 people fled their homes in the past week alone, a U.N. agency estimated on Friday, some with little more than the clothes on their backs.

Al-Megdad Hashem and his family were among them. At first, one night late last week, they stayed home, kept awake by the sound of shelling. Then, the next morning, shells landed near their house, in the fiercely contested province of Taiz, wounding two people, including Mr. Hashem’s nephew.

The only way to get them to a hospital was to load them onto a truck that normally carries construction materials. All told, he said, 34 people piled in, including Mr. Hashem, his wife, their four children and his elderly parents. They had barely enough time to stuff their belongings into one small bag.

“It was difficult to take anything,” he said. “We want the war to stop so that people can return to their homes.”

The civil war had largely settled into a fragile peace in recent years, since a 2022 U.N.-brokered cease-fire effectively partitioned the country between government- and Houthi-held areas. Now, Yemen is again in the throes of full-fledged fighting, aggravating what was already one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

Making matters worse, the U.N. World Food Program is so short of money that it has suspended food aid altogether and reduced its provision of monthly cash assistance to every other month, Carl Skau, the agency’s acting executive director, said in a phone interview on Thursday. He had visited Yemen last week.

Children were not going to school in the camps for displaced people that he visited, he said. Yemenis told him they were selling their belongings to buy food. And at one health clinic, a long line of mothers were waiting to be seen, with malnourished children in their arms. “They were struggling to afford one meal a day,” he said.

Yemen, he said, has been barraged not only by the fighting. The disruption of shipping in the region has also raised food prices in a country that imports most of what it eats. Meanwhile, droughts and floods have damaged Yemen’s farms. “The little they produce inside is turned upside down by the weather,” Mr. Skau said.

Even before the latest surge in violence, an estimated 4.5 million Yemenis were displaced from their homes. Nearly half of the country’s health facilities are not functional. Attacks on aid workers have forced the United Nations to suspend operations in the Houthi-held north.

This week, Houthi forces captured Mokha, a strategic Red Sea port city in Taiz, as well as an island in the waterway, according to two Yemeni officials, giving the militia a foothold in Bab al-Mandab, a major maritime choke point through which oil from Saudi Arabia passes on its way to Asia.

Houthi forces have also attacked Saudi oil facilities, in turn pushing up already rising global oil prices.

The Houthis have frequently accused Saudi Arabia of striking their positions.

On Friday, the broadcaster Al-Masirah, which is controlled by the militia, said that Saudi Arabia had launched two rounds of airstrikes on the port of Mokha. The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment.

The United Nations said on Thursday that at least 14 civilians were killed in the fighting this past week, including two children.

Last Saturday, in the contested Maqbanah district of Taiz Province, Omar Abdulaziz al-Himyari, 25, fled after hearing shelling nearby. At dawn, he and five family members climbed for two hours by foot to a mountain ridge, their route to the closest road. From there they found a car to the nearest city.

“We left in the clothes we were wearing,” he said. “We couldn’t carry anything because of the situation and the difficult terrain.”

They left behind all of their most valuable belongings, including their cows and goats, their beehives and the grain they had planted in their fields.

For now, Mr. al-Himyari is staying with his brother-in-law and looking for work in the city of Taiz, now crowded with the newly displaced. The prices of flour and rice have shot up at the market. Water must be procured from a tanker, and that too is pricey.

“I honestly don’t know how we will manage our daily needs,” he said.

More than 18 million Yemenis face what the United Nations calls acute food insecurity, with 2.2 million children acutely malnourished.

Disease and medical care also remain pressing concerns. The World Health Organization reported more than 17,600 measles cases in the first seven months of the year. At the main hospital in the government-held city of Marib, maternity and obstetric services have been suspended to make space for trauma care, the W.H.O. said, and dead bodies exceed “available mortuary capacity.”

The crisis is especially dire in the Houthi-held north. United Nations operations have been suspended there since October, when U.N. and other aid workers were detained and U.N. offices were raided by the militia. Seventy-three U.N. staff members remain in Houthi detention, the U.N. relief chief told the Security Council in August.

And although Yemen was once a focus of world aid groups, many major funders of relief, such as the United States, have significantly cut their aid budgets.

Yemen needs $2.2 billion in humanitarian assistance, according to the U.N. relief agency, which said it had received only 20 percent of that.

item.title: In Flood-Stricken Nepal, a Cool Gust Carries Hopes of a Miracle Rescue
item.description:
Deep beneath the Himalayas, six men were harnessing the fierce force of glacial melt that provides electricity to Nepal when a terrible deluge struck, filling their workplace, an underground powerhouse, with a churn of silt, rock and water. Floor by floor, life was extinguished.

But two and a half weeks after that devastating flooding, rescue crews digging through a silt-swamped tunnel at the Chilime hydropower project have made a tantalizing discovery. The area toward the top of the five-floor underground facility appears to be fed by a pocket of air.

In a drowned and battered landscape, the presence of oxygen, cool and fresh according to rescue workers, lit faint hopes that the six workers — the only ones still unaccounted for at the facility — might have somehow survived.

Chances of life are still slim. While three workers were pulled out of tunnels at other hydropower projects on the ninth and 10th days after the floods, another week has now passed. The floods have killed at least 1,385 people in Nepal and left 5,130 missing, along with hundreds more unaccounted for in neighboring Tibet.
